extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers; students of moral philosophy; readers of Montaigne-style essays
extracted.subtask_description: An introspective, discursive essay form treating moral, practical, and philosophical topics by example and reflection rather than systematic argument. The page is a Renaissance-style personal essay exploring human character, vice, and conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action should be guided by a determinate end
rubrics_metrics.description: “No one lays down a certain design for his life, and we only deliberate thereof by pieces. The archer ought first to know at what he is to aim, and then accommodate his arm... No wind serves him who addresses his voyage to no certain, port.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate plans, counsels, or actions by whether they are aligned to a clear, conceived goal. Examples/advice: an archer must know his target; voyages require a defined port. Warning: counsel and efforts that lack a determinate end deviate and wander.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not judge solely by outward actions—seek inner motives
rubrics_metrics.description: “...it is not all the understanding has to do, simply to judge us by our outward actions; it must penetrate the very soul, and there discover by what springs the motion is guided.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess people and actions by intended motives and internal drives, not only by external behaviour. Note the author calls this a 'high and hazardous undertaking' and suggests caution—fewer should attempt penetrating inner motives because of difficulty and risk of error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vices differ in kind and degree — evaluate by effect on soul vs body
rubrics_metrics.description: “The world is nothing but variety and disemblance, vices are all alike, as they are vices... yet they are not all equal vices... The soul has greater part in the rest, and there are some vices that have something, if a man may so say, of generous in them; this one [drunkenness] is totally corporeal and earthly.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging vices, distinguish those that involve intellect, courage, or skill (which may include mixed qualities) from wholly physical or degrading vices. Drunkenness is presented as particularly brutish because it 'overthrows' the soul and reduces the person to physical stupor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider loss of self-government and disclosure of secrets as harms of drunkenness
rubrics_metrics.description: “The worst state of man is that wherein he loses the knowledge and government of himself... wine, in those who have drunk beyond measure, vents the most inward secrets.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate excess drinking by its tendency to undermine self-control and to cause disclosure of private confidences (supported by historical/anecdotal examples like Josephus' ambassador and Augustus' confidants).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual and role-based restrictions on drinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato's injunctions and related ancient prescriptions: forbids children wine till eighteen, forbids drunkenness till forty, allows later liberal use; prohibits drinking in public duty contexts—judges/magistrates should abstain, day reserved for work, certain nights reserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge acceptable drinking practices against role, age, and social function: public office, judicial duties, military expeditions, and days intended for other purposes are unsuitable for intoxication. Use historical precedent (Plato, Stoics) as guidance for moderation tied to duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation and frequency as measures of acceptable drinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of drinking 'after the French fashion' (two meals, moderate) as too sparing, and praise of more frequent convivial drinking in ancient customs; yet author warns against delicate palate and recommends indifference in taste for abundant pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate drinking habits by balance between moderation and convivial frequency. The author both criticises overly rare indulgence and cautions against refined taste that makes one suffer when only poor wine is available—recommendation: temperance in quality-sensitivity to preserve pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise human frailty—virtue requires moderation, not impossible constancy
rubrics_metrics.description: “The most regular and most perfect soul in the world has but too much to do to keep itself upright... Wisdom does not force our natural dispositions... ‘Tis sufficient for a man to curb and moderate his inclinations, for totally to suppress them is not in him to do.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims of extreme constancy or Stoic invulnerability skeptically: accept that human passions and bodily conditions can overcome reason. Virtue should be judged by moderation and self-curbing rather than absolute suppression of natural impulses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish truly courageous endurance from cowardly evasion (esp. regarding suicide)
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument that 'There is more constancy in suffering the chain we are tied to than in breaking it, and more pregnant evidence of fortitude in Regulus than in Cato'—and that fleeing life often reflects cowardice, not virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating acts regarding life and death, prefer evidence of enduring hardship in service or duty as higher virtue than choosing death to evade adversity. Use historical exemplars (Regulus, Cato) and Stoic debates to weigh whether suicide is an act of fortitude or of impatience/cowardice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for duties to others and divine/societal law when judging suicide
rubrics_metrics.description: Opposing view: some argue we cannot quit the world without God's command or regard for country and laws; 'we are not born for ourselves only, but for our country also, the laws of which require an account from us.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate proposals for self-harm against obligations to God, community, and law. Consider legal/religious consequences (honour or ignominy at burial) and social duties as limiting permissible grounds for suicide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware fear of future harms causing worse present harms
rubrics_metrics.description: “The fear of future ills often makes men run into extreme danger; he is truly brave who boldly dares withstand the mischiefs he apprehends..." and examples: people who, fearing death, throw themselves into it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess decisions driven by anticipatory fear critically: fear of potential harms can produce irrational actions that worsen outcomes. As a criterion, evaluate whether action is motivated by prudent forethought or by panic-driven avoidance that invites the very danger feared.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use historical/anecdotal examples to test moral claims but with caution
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay repeatedly invokes historical anecdotes and literary citations (e.g., Attalus & Pausanias, Augustus & Piso, Plato, Stoics, Roman exempla) to illustrate points about vice, virtue, and human frailty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a method for evaluating moral claims, weigh illustrative historical examples for their instructive value but be cautious about generalising from exceptional cases. The author uses anecdotes both to warn and to nuance positions (e.g., some drunk yet reliable figures).
